summary: Opheltes (Ancient Greek: Ὀφέλτης), also called Archemorus ("Beginning of Doom"), was the infant son of Lycurgus of Nemea — by Eurydice, Amphithea, or the nymph Nemea — killed by a serpent when his nurse Hypsipyle set him down to guide the Seven against Thebes to water. Amphiaraus renamed him Archemorus as an omen of the Seven's doom; funeral games in his honor became the origin of the Nemean Games.
etymology: Ancient Greek Opheltēs (Ὀφέλτης). The ritual name Archemorus (Ἀρχέμορος) means "beginning of doom" — Amphiaraus's reading of the infant's death as portent of the Seven's fate at Thebes.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Euripides and Statius make his parents Lycurgus — priest and/or king of Nemea — and Eurydice. Apollodorus agrees (Lycurgus son of Pheres), adding "or, as some say, Amphithea"; Hyginus's Latin "Lycus" is probably a slip for Lycurgus. Aeschylus, per Pindar scholia, makes the mother the eponymous nymph Nemea. Keep this Nemean infant distinct from other Opheltes figures (e.g. the Peneleid).

sections.heading: Death and the Nemean Games
paragraphs: On the road to Thebes the Seven need water at Nemea and meet Hypsipyle, nurse of Opheltes. While she leads them to a spring she lays the child on the ground; a serpent kills him. The Seven slay the snake; Amphiaraus renames the boy Archemorus and reads the omen. They hold funeral games that tradition makes the founding of the Nemean Games.

sections.heading: Heroön at Nemea
paragraphs: Pausanias saw a "grave of Opheltes" with altars inside a stone wall, and nearby a mound he took for Lycurgus's tomb. Excavations by the University of California (from 1979) identified an Archaic open-air precinct about a hundred metres southwest of the Temple of Zeus as the likely heroön.
